```{r}
#| warning: false
library(survival)
```

## Learning Objective

Interpret the coefficients of a Cox proportional hazards model with an
interaction term.


## Lesson

Since you've learned how to interpret interaction terms
in linear, logistic, and Poisson regression,
I'm sure you can do it with Cox regression.
Let's dive directly into an example.

```{r}
d_colon <- colon

# Just death, not recurrence
d_colon <- d_colon[d_colon$etype == 2, ]
d_colon$age_50 <- d_colon$age - 50
```

These are the variables for the colon cancer example:

- `time`: Time until death in days. Unfortunately, I don't know the time origin.
- `status`: 1 is death, 0 is censoring.
- `rx`: This is the treatment variable, and it has three levels:
`Obs` for observation; `Lev` for Levamisole,
and `Lev+5FU` for Levamisole plus 5-FU.
- `sex`: 1 for male, 0 for female.
- `age_50`: This is in years minus 50, but I don't know when it was measured.
Maybe at the time origin?

The results of a Cox regression is below.

```{r}
#| echo: true
# Cox regression
mod_01 <- coxph(formula = Surv(time = time,
                               event = status) ~ rx * age_50 + sex,
                data = d_colon)
summary(mod_01)
```

How do we interpret these coefficients?

**Main Effects**

- Among people who are 50 years old and are of the same sex,
the hazard rate for people prescribed Levamisole
is about 8% lower than the hazard rate for people on observation only.
- Among people who are 50 years old and are of the same sex,
the hazard rate for people prescribed Levamisole plus 5-FU
is about 22% lower than the hazard rate for people on observation only.
- Among people on observation and are of the same sex,
each additional year of age is associated with a 0.47% increase
in the hazard rate.
- The hazard rate among males is 0.42% lower than the hazard rate among
females,
holding treatment and age constant.

**Effect of Treatment at Different Ages**

- Among people who are 51 years old and are of the same sex,
the hazard rate for people prescribed Levamisole
is about $0.9238 \times 1.0049 = 0.9283266$ times
the hazard rate for people on observation only.
- Among people who are 51 years old and are of the same sex,
the hazard rate for people prescribed Levamisole plus 5-FU
is about $0.7811 \times 0.9869 = 0.7708676$ times
the hazard rate for people on observation only.

**Effect of Age for Different Treatments**

- Among people prescribed Levamisole and who are of the same sex,
each additional year of age is associated with a 0.96% increase
in the hazard rate,
since $1.0047 \times 1.0049 = 1.009623$.
- Among people prescribed Levamisole plus 5-FU and who are of the same sex,
each additional year of age is associated with a 0.85% decrease
in the hazard rate,
since $1.0047 \times 0.9869 = 0.9915384$.


## Problems

### Problem 1

Let's return to the diabetic retinopathy data set.
The explanatory variables are as follows:

- `trt`: Treatment (0 = no treatment, 1 = laser).
- `laser`: The two levels are argon and xenon.

Note that I've added a new explanatory variable, `laser`.
This is the type of laser that the person was assigned to.
In this study, each person was assigned to either argon or xenon;
then, one eye was randomly selected to receive treatment.
The other eye went untreated.

For the analysis below, I've only used the left eye for each person.
For some of these people,
we are observing the untreated eye,
even though the person was assigned to one of the two lasers.




#### Part (a)

Interpret the estimated coefficients in this Cox regression model:
```{r}
d_dr <- diabetic
d_dr <- d_dr[d_dr$eye == "left", ]
mod_02 <- coxph(formula = Surv(time = time,
                               event = status) ~ trt * laser,
                data = d_dr)
summary(mod_02)
```


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

- Eyes treated with xenon have a 58% lower hazard rate than untreated
eyes belonging to people assigned to xenon.
- Untreated eyes belonging to people assigned to argon have a 31% higher hazard rate
than untreated eyes belonging to people assigned to xenon.
- Eyes treated with argon have an 87% lower hazard rate than untreated eyes
belonging to people assigned to argon,
since $0.4235 \times 0.2989 = 0.1265842$.
- Eyes treated with argon have a 61% lower hazard rate than eyes treated
with xenon, since $1.3062 \times 0.2989 = 0.3904232$.

:::

#### Part (b)

Interpret the estimated coefficients in this Cox regression model:
```{r}
mod_03 <- coxph(formula = Surv(time = time,
                               event = status) ~ trt + trt:laser,
                data = d_dr)
summary(mod_03)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

This might require some explanation.
Our model is
$$
\hat{h}_i(t) = \hat{h}_0(t) \exp\left( -0.9667\texttt{trt} - 0.9403 \texttt{trt}\times \texttt{laserargon}\right) \text{.}
$$

The estimated hazard at time $t$ for an untreated eye is
$$
\begin{align*}
\hat{h}_i(t) &= \hat{h}_0(t) \exp\left( -0.9667 (0) - 0.9403 (0)\times \texttt{laserargon}\right) \\
&= \hat{h}_0(t) \text{.}
\end{align*}
$$

The estimated hazard at time $t$ for an eye treated with xenon is
$$
\begin{align*}
\hat{h}_i(t) &= \hat{h}_0(t) \exp\left( -0.9667 (1) - 0.9403 (1)\times (0)\right) \\
&= \hat{h}_0(t) \exp\left( -0.9667 \right) \text{.}
\end{align*}
$$

The estimated hazard at time $t$ for an eye treated with argon is
$$
\begin{align*}
\hat{h}_i(t) &= \hat{h}_0(t) \exp\left( -0.9667 (1) - 0.9403 (1)\times (1)\right) \\
&= \hat{h}_0(t) \exp\left( -0.9667 - 0.9403 \right) \text{.}
\end{align*}
$$

This leads to the following interpretations:

- Eyes treated with xenon have a 62% lower hazard rate than untreated eyes.
- Eyes treated with argon have an 85% lower hazard rate than untreated eyes,
since $0.3803 \times 0.3905 = 0.1485072$.

:::

#### Part (c)

Which model is better, the one with `laserargon` or the one without?
Or, is there a third model that would surpass both?
Justify your answer.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The model with `laserargon` allows for untreated eyes assigned to argon
to differ from untreated eyes assigned to xenon.
I don't think there's a good reason to believe these two groups of eyes
would differ, since both are untreated.
In the model, we see that the p-value for `laserargon` is high,
meaning the difference is not statistically significant.
This is an argument for leaving out that variable.

I would argue, though, that
the best thing to do would be to include both eyes for each person.
That way, each person could serve as their own control.
Including both eyes would violate the independence assumption, though,
so to do that we would need methods that aren't covered in this class.

:::
